p: heaviness: Causing grief among you, which he would have done if he had come to them before they had repented.
confidence in you all: For I trusted that you would immediately take that out of the way which you knew I was discontented with, considering how you are persuaded that my joy is your joy.

But if any have caused grief: He passes to another part of this epistle: which nonetheless is put among the first, and to which he returns afterwards: and he handles the releasing and unloosing of the incestuous person, because he seemed to have been given sufficient testimony of his repentance. And this shows the true use of excommunication, that is, that it proceeds not from hatred, but from love, and so end, lest if we keep it up, we serve Satan the devil.
grieved me: As if he said, "All that sorrow is so completely wiped away, that I have never felt it."
in part: As for me, says Paul, I have no more to do with him.
overcharge you all: Lest I should overcharge him who is burdened enough as it is, which burden I would be glad if it were taken from him.
forgive him: That whereas before you punished him sharply, you should now forgive him.
confirm your love toward him: That at my entreaty you would declare by the consent of the whole church, that you take him again as a brother.
person of Christ: Truly, and from the heart.
devices: Of his mischievous counsel and devilish will.
Furthermore: He returns to the confirmation of his apostleship, and brings forth both the testimonies of his labours, and also of God's blessing.
savour of his knowledge by us: He alludes to the anointing of the priests, and the incense of the sacrifices.

For we are unto God a: He denies that anything should be taken away from the dignity of his apostleship, because they saw that it was not received with like success in every place. But rather very many rejected and detested him, seeing that he preached Christ not only as a saviour of those that believe, but also as a judge of those that condemn him.

And who is sufficient for these: Again, he dismisses all suspicion of arrogance, attributing all things that he did to the power of God, whom he serves sincerely, and with honest affection. And he makes them witnesses of this, even to the sixth verse of the next chapter 2Co 2:17 - 3:6.

corrupt the word of God: We do not handle it craftily and covetously, or less sincerely than we ought. And he uses a metaphor, which is taken from hucksters, who used to play the false harlot with whatever came into their hands.
